title: The Appendix: No Respect
summary: The Appendix: No Respect is a Stuff You Should Know episode (an Appendix/"Appendix" installment published 2021-05-04) in which Josh and Chuck (with Jerry in the studio) discuss the appendix as an organ. They cover its location at the cecum, the long-held vestigial-organ idea tied to Charles Darwin, the 2007 Duke University "safe house" theory for gut bacteria, the appendix's role in producing immune cells, the hygiene hypothesis and rising appendicitis in developing countries, appendicitis causes and symptoms, the history of appendectomy and Reginald Fitz's 1886 identification, negative appendectomies, and Harry Houdini's death from a ruptured appendix. The episode closes with a listener mail from a ten-year-old listener, Jack, suggesting a child labor episode.

segments.title: Opening banter and studio reunion
segments.summary: The hosts reunite in the studio for the first time in about fourteen months, joke about champagne and a frozen shrimp cocktail, and chat about weight gain during the pandemic before previewing the appendix topic.

segments.title: What the appendix is and its location
segments.summary: The hosts describe the appendix as a worm-like pouch hanging off the cecum where the small and large intestines meet, note its typical two to four inch length and the record ten-inch appendix from an autopsy, and discuss that it has no obvious role in digestion.

segments.title: Appendix in other mammals and gut microbes
segments.summary: The hosts explain that herbivores have large cecums used to predigest plant fiber, describe the role of gut microbes in breaking down cellulose and fiber, and mention that only about fifty of 361 mammal species have an appendix-like organ, with wombats noted for cube-shaped poop.

segments.title: Vestigial organ idea and Darwin
segments.summary: The hosts explain that the appendix was long considered a vestigial organ, credited to Charles Darwin's idea that the cecum shrank as human diets changed. They note the appendix was named by Philippe Verheyen in 1710 and that appendectomies were performed as early as 1735. The idea was believed for over 150 years and seemed to be supported by safe removal of the organ.

segments.title: Safe house theory from Duke University
segments.summary: The hosts describe the 2007 Duke University findings proposing that the appendix acts as a safe house for good gut bacteria, which repopulate the large intestine after diarrheal illness, and that the appendix also produces immune cells such as lymphocytes.

segments.title: Hygiene hypothesis and appendicitis rates
segments.summary: The hosts link the appendix's role to the hygiene hypothesis, arguing that an overactive immune system in sanitary environments may attack the appendix. They note appendicitis rates rose in the United States and Europe in the early twentieth century and in developing countries as they industrialized.

segments.title: Appendicitis causes, symptoms, and appendectomy history
segments.summary: The hosts explain appendicitis as a blockage of the appendix's narrow opening by bacteria, seeds, or fecaliths, leading to inflammation, and describe symptoms and where the pain is felt. They cover Reginald Fitz's identification of the disease in 1886, the first appendectomy by Thomas Morton, and the risk of rupture leading to peritonitis, with a mortality rate of roughly 0.2 to 0.8 percent.

segments.title: Negative appendectomies and observation
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the newer call for doctors to avoid negative appendectomies, suggesting a non-perforated appendix may resolve on its own, and advise anyone with concerning abdominal pain to see a doctor.

segments.title: Harry Houdini's death from appendicitis
segments.summary: The hosts describe how Harry Houdini died of a ruptured appendix after a college student punched his stomach in 1926, noting that scholars believe he already had appendicitis, and mention Houdini's influence on their interest in magic.

segments.title: Listener mail from Jack about child labor
segments.summary: A ten-year-old listener named Jack from Hiawatha, Iowa, praises the Titanic episode and suggests an episode on child labor. The hosts respond warmly and promise it is coming.
